documents.text:
195 FERC ¶ 61,217
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ADDRESSING ARGUMENTS RAISED ON REHEARING AND SETTING ASIDE PRIOR ORDER, IN PART

(Issued June 18, 2026)

On January 29, 2026, the Commission issued an order granting a certificate of public convenience and necessity (Certificate Order) to Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line Company, LLC (Transco), authorizing Transco to construct and operate new pipeline and compression facilities, and modify and replace existing facilities, in Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama as part of Transco’s Southeast Supply Enhancement Project (SSE Project).  On February 27, 2026, Transco filed a request for rehearing of the Certificate Order.  On March 2, 2026, a group of organizations and two landowners (Petitioners) filed a joint request for rehearing.
Pursuant to Allegheny Defense Project v. FERC, the rehearing requests filed in this proceeding may be deemed denied by operation of law.  However, as permitted by Natural Gast Act (NGA) section 19(a), we are modifying the discussion in the Certificate Order and setting aside the Certificate Order, in part, as discussed below.
Background
The SSE Project is designed to provide up to 1,596,900 Dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of incremental firm transportation capacity from Transco’s existing Station 165 Zone 5 Pooling Point and the Cherrystone Interconnect with Mountain Valley Pipeline, LLC (MVP) in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, to natural gas markets in the southeast United States.
Transco held a non-binding open season and reverse open season for the SSE Project from June 19, 2023 through July 14, 2023, which resulted in Transco executing ten precedent agreements for 100% of the project capacity at negotiated rates with: Atlanta Gas Light Company for 75,000 Dth/d; City of Danville for 1,500 Dth/d; City of Fountain Inn for 2,400 Dth/d; City of Wilson for 2,000 Dth/d; Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (Duke Energy) for 1,000,000 Dth/d; Fort Hill Natural Gas Authority for 5,000 Dth/d; Greer Commission of Public Works for 10,000 Dth/d; Municipal Gas Authority of Georgia for 2,000 Dth/d; Patriots Energy Group for 14,000 Dth/d; South Carolina Public Service Authority for 80,000 Dth/d; Southern Company Services, Inc. (Southern Company) for 400,000 Dth/d; and Southwestern Virginia Gas Company for 5,000 Dth/d.
On October 29, 2024, Transco submitted an application requesting authorization to construct, operate, and maintain the SSE Project pursuant to NGA sections 7(b) and 7(c) (Application).  Public notice of the Application was published in the Federal Register on November 18, 2024, which provided a deadline for intervention, comments and protests of December 3, 2024.
On June 24, 2025, Transco submitted a market study prepared by Levitan & Associates, Inc. (Levitan Study) addressing need for the project.  The Levitan Study, among other things, forecasts unprecedented electricity demand growth across the Southeast region driven largely by expanding large loads, including data centers and manufacturing facilities, and observes that additional gas infrastructure is needed to support gas-fired generation and meet supply diversity and fuel security needs during critical periods and for meeting seasonal peak demand.
On July 16, 2025, certain Petitioners filed a London Economics, Inc. report titled “Uncertainty and Upward Bias Are Inherent in Data Center Electricity Demand Projections” (LEI Report) identifying a phantom load problem where “data center developers have incentives to submit multiple, redundant interconnection requests ... creating a structural upward bias in forecasts” and claiming that “the global supply chain of semiconductor chips is inadequate to support projected data center demand.”
On September 12, 2025, Transco filed a supplement to the Levitan Study prepared by the study authors which analyzed and responded to the LEI Report claims regarding overstated demand in the Southeast U.S.
On October 31, 2025, pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Commission staff issued an Environmental Assessment (EA) for the SSE Project disclosing the potential environmental impacts of the project and concluding that approval of the SSE Project would not constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.  The Commission issued public notice of the EA and set a December 1, 2025 deadline for comments.  Petitioners filed joint comments on the EA on December 1, 2025.
On December 22, 2025, Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, Appalachian Voices, 7 Directions of Service, and Katie Whitehead filed a Motion to Lodge a report prepared by Greenlink Analytics and Science for Georgia (Greenlink Report) and comments alleging that the Greenlink Report “undermine[s] utility shippers’ purported need for additional gas transportation capacity.”  Specifically, the December 22 Comments & Motion alleged that the Greenlink Report contained new evidence casting doubt on the data-center-driven natural gas demand growth projected by Transco and the project shippers.  Transco and Duke Energy filed answers to the December 22 Comments & Motion on December 29, 2025 and January 5, 2026, respectively.
On January 29, 2026, the Commission issued the Certificate Order authorizing Transco to construct and operate the SSE Project, finding that “Transco has demonstrated a need for the proposed project, which will provide 1,596,900 Dth/d of firm transportation service ... [and] will not have adverse impacts on Transco’s existing shippers or other pipelines and their existing customers.”  The Commission also found that the project’s benefits will outweigh any adverse effects on landowners and surrounding communities.  And although the project would impact the environment and individuals living in the vicinity of the project facilities, the Commission determined that the project impacts, as mitigated, would not be significant.  Based on these findings, the Commission concluded that “under section 7 of the NGA ... the public convenience and necessity requires approval of [the] project, subject to ... conditions.”
On February 27, 2026, Transco filed a request for rehearing of certain rate-related aspects of the Certificate Order.  On March 2, 2026, Petitioners filed a request for rehearing of certain public interest findings and environmental matters considered in the Certificate Order.  On April 10, 2026, Transco filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to the Petitioners’ request for rehearing.
On April 23, 2026, Petitioners filed a motion to stay the Commission’s Certificate Order and Notice to Proceed, which the Commission denied on May 14, 2026.  Petitioners also filed a motion for stay pending judicial review with the D.C. Circuit, which the court denied on June 5, 2026 finding that “[o]n the merits, the environmental petitioners have not demonstrated that they will likely succeed in showing that [the Commission’s] consideration of ... environmental effects fell outside a broad zone of reasonableness.”
Procedural Matters
The Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure prohibit answers to a request for rehearing.  Accordingly, we deny Transco’s April 10, 2026 motion to answer and reject the answer.
Petitioners’ Rehearing Request includes voluminous supplemental attachments.  Rule 713 of our Rules of Practice and Procedure states that any rehearing request must “[s]et forth the matters relied upon by the party requesting rehearing, if rehearing is sought based on matters not available for consideration by the Commission at the time of the final decision or final order.”  The Commission does not allow parties to provide new information on rehearing because it raises fairness and due process concerns as other parties are precluded from filing answers in response.  Further, the Commission has long held that “parties are not permitted to introduce new evidence for the first time on rehearing since such practice would allow an impermissible moving target … and would frustrate needed administrative finality.”
Although some of Petitioners’ supplements appear to be duplicative of information previously accepted into the record in the underlying proceeding, Petitioners do not explain whether the bulk of the 34 attachments contains new information.  To the extent there are new materials, Petitioners similarly do not justify their delay in waiting until the rehearing stage to submit these materials.  For these reasons, we reject the attachments.  Nevertheless, as explained below, based on information previously accepted into the record, we continue to find the Commission’s review and approval of the SSE Project appropriate.
Next, we address the procedural posture of the December 22 Comments & Motion, which sought to enter the Greenlink Report and related arguments into the record.  As discussed above, on December 22, 2025, Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, Appalachian Voices, 7 Directions of Service, Katie Whitehead, and Robert McNutt filed the December 22 Comments & Motion, and attached the Greenlink Report, in the proceeding.  On rehearing, Petitioners argue that the “Commission’s decision to not consider” the Greenlink Report and lack of a “reasoned justification for refusing to consider... [the] Motion” violates the Commission’s obligations under the NGA because “the Commission may approve a new interstate pipeline project only if it ‘is or will be required by the present or future public convenience and necessity’” based on “all relevant factors reflecting on the need for the project.”  Petitioners further allege that the Commission failed to provide an “applicable, governing deadline” or “reasonable standard” for rejecting the Greenlink Report, while continuing to accept filings from Transco, and failed to explain why the timing of Petitioners’ filing either prevented Commission consideration or “would have prejudiced the project applicant or another party in any way.”  We disagree.
In the Certificate Order, the Commission explained that “[t]he report was filed over a year after the close of the comment period established by the Notice of Application” and that the “movants offer[ed] no justification for why their filing was so delayed.”  Specifically, the Commission set a deadline of December 3, 2024 for comments, yet Petitioners did not file the report before that deadline.  Instead, as noted in the Certificate Order, Petitioners waited until after expiration of the December 1, 2025 deadline for comments on the EA to file the December 22 Comments & Motion and Greenlink Report.  Petitioners continue to provide no justification for their delay, nor do they provide any compelling justification for acceptance of the December 22 Comments & Motion and Greenlink Report at an extremely late stage of the proceeding.  Rather, Petitioners allege that the Commission acted without “identify[ing] any applicable deadline [they] failed to meet .... [and] did not suggest that the timing of the filing prevented the Commission from considering the evidence.”  However, as noted above and in the Certificate Order, the Commission provided notice of the deadline for protests in this proceeding in the Federal Register on November 18, 2024.  As explained in the Certificate Order, the December 22 Comments & Motion, and the accompanying Greenlink Report, were filed over a year after the close of the comment period.
Additionally, the conclusion of the Commission’s NEPA process often signals that the administrative process is nearing its end, with the Commission often acting within just a couple months of concluding its environmental reviews.  These facts belie the assertions by Petitioners, who include multiple experienced Commission litigants, that the Commission did not set a deadline for comments and they “are aware of none.”
Under these circumstances, we sustain the Commission’s decision to deny the December 22 Comments & Motion and reject the untimely Greenlink Report.  The Commission has broad discretion on how to structure its proceedings.  Petitioners’ December 22 Comments & Motion and associated Greenlink Report were unquestionably late, not supported by good cause explaining the reason for the delay, and acceptance would have unreasonably interrupted the administrative process.  Petitioners waited until late December to file detailed technical information and market-related arguments which would have required the Commission to considerably delay the proceeding to consider not only Petitioners’ additional arguments but also two separate answers in response.  This would have unduly prejudiced the applicant, the SSE Project shippers, and their customers, all of whom are relying on the timely availability of project capacity.  Accordingly, we sustain our decision to deny Petitioners’ motion to lodge and dismiss the remainder of Petitioners’ substantive Greenlink Report-based claims as moot.  Nevertheless, in the alternative, we further explain below why the Greenlink Report would not alter the Commission’s conclusion that the SSE Project is supported by market need and required by the public convenience and necessity.
Finally, Petitioners’ request that the Commission rescind the Notice to Proceed with Construction dated February 25, 2026 (Notice to Proceed) and “order the stop of any construction activities” because precedent requires that the Commission “strictly enforce its pre-construction conditions to avoid an asymmetrical regime allowing construction to begin before parties can be afforded timely access to judicial review.”  Petitioners also generally allege that tree felling associated with initial construction will cause irreparable harm.
Although Petitioners’ request was not accompanied by a motion to stay the Notice to Proceed, on April 23, 2026, Petitioners filed a motion to stay the Commission’s Certificate Order and Notice to Proceed, which the Commission denied in an order issued May 14, 2026.  As explained in the Commission’s Stay Order, Petitioners did not demonstrate that irreparable injury would occur absent a stay halting construction.  Conversely, the Commission determined that granting a stay would cause delay and therefore substantial harm to Transco and its customers who are relying on the SSE Project to provide needed transportation service.  Ultimately, the Commission concluded that the public interest did not support granting a stay.  Because Petitioners’ claims were addressed in the Stay Order, they are dismissed here as moot.
Further, as explained in the Notice to Proceed, Commission staff determined that Transco had provided information necessary to meet applicable pre-construction conditions of the Certificate Order, and staff confirmed the receipt of all other federal authorizations relevant to the approved activities.  Petitioners do not dispute these findings.  In any event, the Commission properly does not delay construction upon satisfaction of applicable conditions.  As the Commission explained in Order No. 915, which rescinded 18 C.F.R. § 157.23 of its regulations, “delaying the issuance of construction authorizations for approved projects ... is no longer in the public interest.”  Specifically, the Commission explained that recission was required “to reduce construction delays resulting from the regulation’s limitation on the issuance of construction authorizations, as well as to promote and expedite efficient energy development and ensure that there is sufficient natural gas infrastructure to timely address resource adequacy and reliability concerns.”  The Commission explained further, “[i]n light of the protections provided by Allegheny and the Commission’s evaluation of a proposed project’s alleged harms” section “157.23 [was] no longer necessary” and that “the protection offered by judicial review and the potential for other case-by-case relief ... are sufficient given that the projects ... have been found to be needed and in the public interest following a fulsome agency review that includes environmental review and consideration of alternatives.”
Discussion
Rates
Transco contends that the Commission erred in the Certificate Order by finding, sua sponte, that the SSE Project qualifies for a predetermination of rolled-in rate treatment.  Specifically, Transco explains that had the Commission used Transco’s “actual zonal system rate design and the correct incremental project cost-of-service, the SSE Project’s incremental revenues would be less than the incremental project costs, indicating that it does not qualify for the predetermination.”
According to Transco, the Commission “overstate[d] the project’s incremental revenues” by applying Transco’s Zone 4-5 Settlement non-incremental system recourse rate of $0.48657 per Dth to all 1,596,900 Dth/d of the SSE Project’s incremental firm capacity instead of applying Transco’s Zone 4-5 system recourse rate to the 1,288,400 Dth/d of incremental capacity created between Zones 4 and 5 and the Zone 5-5 system recourse rate of 0.22688 per Dth to the 308,500 Dth/d of incremental capacity created within Zone 5.  Transco also contends that the Commission omitted $2,464,183 in variable costs associated with the usage charge from the incremental project cost of service used in making its predetermination finding.  We agree, and set aside the Certificate Order, in part, as discussed below.
As explained in the Certificate Order, to receive a predetermination favoring rolled-in rate treatment, a pipeline must demonstrate that rolling in the costs associated with the construction and operation of new facilities will not result in existing customers subsidizing the expansion.  In general, this means that a pipeline must show that the revenues to be generated by an expansion project will exceed the project costs.  To make this determination, we compare the cost of the project to the revenues generated using actual contract volumes at either the maximum recourse rate or, if the negotiated rate is lower than the recourse rate, the actual negotiated rate.
Upon further consideration, we find that the SSE Project would not qualify for a predetermination of rolled in rate treatment because the incremental revenues from the SSE Project would not exceed the incremental cost of service.  On December 2, 2025, to reflect recent certification of Transco’s uncontested rate case settlement in Docket Nos. RP24-1035-000 and RP24-1035-004 (Settlement), staff required Transco to recalculate the proposed incremental rates for the SSE Project and “provide a comparison to the relevant system rates that would otherwise apply” under the Settlement.  On December 10, 2025, Transco provided recalculated incremental rates “utilizing cost factors from the [Settlement],” which resulted in a reduction in proposed incremental rates.  The Commission approved the Settlement on December 30, 2025.
In the Certificate Order, the Commission considered the recalculated proposed incremental project rates and found that “[t]he revised incremental rate for the project is ... lower than the system rate resulting from the Settlement, and ... direct[ed] Transco to use the system rate contained in the Settlement as the project recourse rate for the expansion capacity,” consistent with Commission policy.
The Commission in the Certificate Order also evaluated whether the expansion project costs qualified for a pre-determination of rolled-in rate treatment based on the new Settlement rates.  Specifically, the Commission calculated incremental revenues for the project “based on the actual volumes of the negotiated agreements with project shippers (1,596,900 Dth/d) and Transco’s Zone 4-5 Settlement recourse rate.”  The Commission explained that the Zone 4-5 Settlement recourse rate was used because it is “lower than the estimated, weighted negotiated rate” for the project.  After finding that the project incremental revenues would exceed the incremental cost of the project in the first year of service, the Commission granted Transco a predetermination to roll the expansion project costs of the SSE Project into its system rates in a future NGA section 4 rate case.
However, as Transco notes, the Zone 4-5 Settlement recourse rate that the Commission used in its calculation is only applicable to a portion of the total SSE Project capacity (1,288,400 Dth/d).  The remainder of the SSE Project capacity (308,500 Dth/d) is subject to the Zone 5-5 system recourse rate, which is lower than the Zone 4-5 Settlement recourse rate.  To correct this oversight, we have adjusted our calculation of incremental revenues to reflect the lower recourse rate applicable to project capacity within Zone 5, which reduces first year incremental revenues from $283,606,326 to $254,364,583.
We also agree that the Certificate Order’s cost of service calculations did not account for Transco’s updated variable costs associated with the usage charge from the incremental project cost of service.  These costs were reflected in Transco’s Data Request Response but were omitted from the total incremental cost of the project in the Certificate Order.  Accordingly, the Certificate Order should have reflected a total incremental cost of service of $264,036,274, as opposed to $261,572,091, for purposes of the Commission’s predetermination analysis.
As clarified above, we find that incremental revenues from the first year of service for the project of $254,364,583 fall below the estimated first year incremental project cost of $264,036,274.  Accordingly, the SSE Project is ineligible for a predetermination of rolled-in rate treatment under the Commission’s Certificate Policy Statement.
This determination is without prejudice to Transco proposing rolled-in rate treatment in a future rate case.  As noted in the Certificate Order, the Commission will require Transco to keep separate books and accounting of costs and revenues attributable to the capacity created by the SSE Project in the same manner as required by section 154.309 of the Commission’s regulations.
Project Need
In their rehearing request, Petitioners contend that the Commission’s “refusal to consider the market need evidence and argument contained in the Motion ... and substantiated by the Greenlink Report violated FERC’s obligations under the NGA” and is inconsistent with the Commission’s “customary practice.”  Petitioners also argue that the Certificate Policy Statement requires that the Commission consider “all relevant factors reflecting on the need for the project.”  Petitioners further claim that the record lacks “concrete evidence of market need” where the Commission “f[ound] the precedent agreements ... dispositive evidence of market need ...; ignor[ed] evidence in the record showing a lack of need; ... refus[ed] to properly consider ... that the [SSE] Project puts ratepayers at risk; and ... dismiss[ed] other evidence ... including an expert report.”  In fact, the Commission did thoroughly examine all relevant factors regarding project need.  We find Petitioners’ arguments unpersuasive and continue to find that Transco has demonstrated that the SSE Project will provide needed natural gas transportation service.
Specifically, Duke Energy and nine other, unaffiliated project shippers consisting of cities, towns, utilities, and other entities have contracted for 100% of the project capacity to serve customer needs.  As the Commission has explained, “[p]recedent agreements for an expansion project’s entire capacity support a finding of project need” and the Commission will “continue to treat precedent agreements as persuasive evidence of market need and will not look beyond them to assess need by other means unless there is credible, contrary evidence discounting their probative value.”  Contrary to Petitioners’ claims, the Certificate Policy Statement does not require that the Commission look behind precedent agreements, which constitute significant evidence of demand for the project.  Although our precedent acknowledges that “market studies may provide evidence of need under the Certificate Policy Statement,” as the Commission has explained, “[p]rojections regarding future demand often change and are influenced by a variety of factors, including economic growth, the cost of natural gas, environmental regulations, and legislative and regulatory decisions by the federal government and individual states” whereas “[a] contract for a pipeline’s capacity is a useful indicator of need because it reflects a ‘business decision’ that such a need exists.”  Indeed, Petitioners concede uncertainty, noting that “projections of data center electricity demand are highly uncertain.” 
By contrast, the Commission has repeatedly affirmed the value of unaffiliated precedent agreements, like the agreements in this proceeding.  The Commission “respect[s] freely-negotiated private contracts” and “absent plausible evidence of         self-dealing between affiliates, the Commission does not look behind precedent agreements to question individual shippers’ business decisions to enter into contracts.”  Petitioners point to no evidence of self-dealing, nor do we find any.
Additionally, in the Certificate Order, the Commission explained that it considered Petitioners’ comments “that there is no market need for the project,” as well as the comments of SSE Project supporters and shippers, and discussed the timely market studies submitted by the parties, but ultimately determined that precedent agreements for 100% of the capacity of the SSE Project supported a finding of market need “[n]otwithstanding the discrepancies between the studies.”  Specifically, the Commission analyzed the Levitan Study assertions of need, the LEI Report claimed “phantom load” problem and the IEEFA report noting the risks of overbuilding in the Certificate Order.  The Certificate Order found that the LEI Report and the IEEFA Report relied on speculative assumptions pertaining to data center demand estimates while the Levitan Study assessed pipeline capacity available to major shippers that have entered into binding precedent agreements and further relied on utility forecasts reviewed by relevant public utility commissions and third-party expert projections, along with broader economic indicators, to conclude that the SSE Project’s additional pipeline capacity is needed through the early 2030s.  And although Petitioners claim that the Commission refused to recognize “attributed evidence” in the LEI Report, we clarify that the Commission nonetheless considered the evidence presented in the LEI Report but found it speculative and outweighed by contrary evidence in the record, including unaffiliated precedent agreements for 100% of the project capacity and utility forecasts. 
Based on this analysis, the Commission found that “while forecasts are inherently subject to uncertainty, state utility regulators are well positioned to vet the input assumptions and criteria used in a forecast, as the state public utility commissions have done here ... [which] forecasts show that electricity demand clearly exists from those facilities.”  Thus, the Commission appropriately concluded that there is not any credible, contrary evidence discrediting the probative value of unaffiliated precedent agreements for 100% of the project capacity.
Next, Petitioners claim that the Commission violated the NGA by “deferring to state public utility commissions’ ... purported endorsement of utility resource plans” and “the fact that the shippers’ inflated demand projections have been reviewed by the North Carolina Utilities Commission (NCUC).”  We disagree, and continue to find that the Commission has met its obligations under NGA section 7.  The Commission’s mandate, and the “principal purpose” of the NGA, is “to encourage the orderly development of plentiful supplies of ... natural gas at reasonable prices.”  Consistent with that obligation, the Commission considered market need for the SSE Project, and based on the existence of unaffiliated precedent agreements for 100% of the project capacity, found sufficient evidence of need.  The Commission also appropriately responded to Petitioners’ state-utility commission-related arguments, without deferring its authority under the NGA.  Specifically, the Commission considered both Petitioners’ state utility commission-related claims and project shippers’ comments in response, and found “electricity demand clearly exists” and noted that this is “reflected in recently state public utility commission-reviewed and approved utility integrated resource plans.”
Further, while Petitioners continue to make general allegations that Duke Energy’s integrated resource plans contain “flawed assumptions,” Petitioners have not adequately explained how their concerns relate to the specific capacity at issue in this proceeding and would have the Commission ignore the fact that the SSE Project capacity was previously incorporated into Duke Energy’s integrated resource plans that were reviewed and approved by its regulators, the NCUC and Public Service Commission of South Carolina, the state public utility commissions with direct oversight over Duke Energy’s state contracting and procurements for distribution customers.
Based on this record, we continue to find that the precedent agreements for 100% of the project capacity executed by ten unaffiliated shippers are the “best evidence that the service to be provided by the project is needed to connect supply and demand, as ... [they] involve parties engaging in negotiations for pipeline transportation services to meet individualized needs.”
Petitioners also make a generalized argument that “the Commission failed to consider the shippers’ ability to pass costs of the [SSE] Project through to captive ratepayers.”  Specifically, Petitioners assert that “Duke, a vertically integrated, investor-owned utility subject to traditional cost-of-service regulation, has a financial incentive to overestimate load growth to justify approval of generation and transmission capacity for which it can recover its costs plus a generous rate of return” and that Southern Company subsidiaries “can recover from captive ratepayers the costs of any capital.”  They reference December 1, 2025 comments filed by certain North Carolina General Assembly members requesting that the Commission “delay a decision” pending issuance of a report being prepared by a state task force, and maintain that this case raises ratepayer concerns similar to those presented in New Jersey Conservation Foundation v. FERC, where the D.C. Circuit faulted the Commission for not considering a state utility board-ordered demand study and concerns raised by state regulators that the capacity was unneeded.  We disagree.
The Certificate Order explained that “state public utilities regulate the rate charged by shippers that are public utilities, and can thus ensure that ratepayers do not subsidize other end users.”  Moreover, the Commission explained that “[t]he forecasts show that electricity demand clearly exists” and noted that this is “reflected in recently state public utility commission-reviewed and approved utility integrated resource plans.”  And we find Petitioners’ reliance on New Jersey Conservation Foundation inapposite here where the Commission’s finding of market need for the Certificate Project, grounded in the precedent agreements, aligns with that of state utility commissions evaluating the subject capacity.  Further, as noted in Transco, shippers’ procurement decisions are “outside the Commission’s jurisdiction and best left to state regulators” where there is no credible evidence of self-dealing because this may “infringe upon the role of state regulators in determining the prudency of expenditures by the utilities they regulate.”  Local distribution company and utility contracts are subject to the scrutiny of state regulatory authorities, and are not within the Commission’s purview.  Accordingly, and consistent with Transco, we find that issues related to incurrence of costs by SSE Project shippers associated with their decisions to subscribe for service on the SSE Project are matters left to the appropriate state utility regulators and are “beyond the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction.”
Accordingly, and as noted above, the Commission’s market need finding is grounded in the NGA, based on an independent assessment of the full record in this proceeding, as articulated in the Certificate Order and further addressed here.
NEPA and Environmental Assertions
Aquatic Resources
Petitioners contend that the Commission’s consideration of impacts to aquatic resources, including cumulative impacts, was deficient and did not comply with its obligations under NEPA and the NGA.  Specifically, Petitioners object to Transco’s use of dry-ditch, open-cut methods for waterbody crossing, contending that trenchless construction methods would be less harmful to the environment, and point to “evidence that nearby pipeline projects found trenchless crossings of certain waterways practicable where Transco did not.”  We find these arguments unpersuasive.
The Commission conducts review of project impacts on a case-specific basis accounting for the unique facts and circumstances present in any given proceeding.  In examining various crossing methods for the SSE Project’s waterbody crossings, including trenchless and open-cut methods, the Certificate Order explains that “Commission staff evaluated Transco’s proposed waterbody crossing procedures and determined that they would be sufficiently protective of the affected waterbodies and in accordance with the Commission’s Wetland and Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures.”  The Commission also noted that “staff consider[ed] the significance of the impact that would be avoided” at each crossing, and ultimately approved the      dry-ditch crossing method after considering crossing method costs and the “significance of the impact that would be avoided.”  The Commission made a case-specific finding that Transco’s proposed “[c]rossing waterbodies using dry-ditch methods would avoid direct in-water work and minimize effects on water quality” and adopted Commission staff’s observation that “on balance” there were no additional waterbodies for which a trenchless crossing technique was warranted.
Contrary to Petitioners’ suggestion, and as demonstrated by the Commission’s reasoning here, because the choice of waterbody crossing method requires balancing of both broader project-specific considerations and narrower site-specific conditions, there is no single best crossing method.  Importantly, the Commission explained that if conditions discovered in the field at a specific waterbody crossing during construction reveal that an alternate crossing method is necessary to minimize impacts, Transco is required to submit a variance request to the Commission for review and approval, including an assessment of the associated environmental impacts.
Next, Petitioners claim that the Commission did not properly consider the cumulative effects of “multiple crossings of a single stream and its tributaries, or multiple crossings within a watershed—here, by [the] SSE [Project] itself and by nearby projects, including MVP Southgate—[which] have synergistic impacts that cannot be captured by analyzing impacts of individual crossings in isolation.”  We disagree.
In the EA, Commission staff identified “172 past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions within the geographic scope of the [SSE] Project ... in [the] cumulative effects analysis, including detailed project descriptions, estimated construction timeframes when available, distance to the proposed [SSE] Project, and resources potentially cumulatively affected.”  Specifically, table H2 in appendix H of the EA analyzed overlapping actions, including impacts associated with cumulative effects on waterbody crossings common between the SSE Project and the MVP Southgate Amendment Project, which “would cross nine of the same named waterbodies ... [and] multiple unnamed tributaries to these named waterbodies.”  Further, the EA provided a “quantitative comparison of overlapping actions occurring within the same HUC-12 subwatersheds” and discussed these cumulative effects in detail in EA Table H3, titled “HUC-12 Watersheds Effects Comparison.”  Table H2 included the Southgate Amendment Project, along with other pipeline projects, as within the scope for consideration of aquatic resources cumulative impacts, and documented 142.6 acres of construction effects, 58.7 acres of operational effects, 15 wetland crossings, and         33 stream crossings that could result in cumulative effects.  Based on this analysis, the EA disclosed that “construction of the Southgate Amendment Project would overlap with Transco’s planned construction schedule” and that “[d]ue to the overlapping workspace and anticipated timeline for Southgate Amendment Project construction, cumulative effects on surface water quality may occur in the affected HUC-12 watersheds ... [t]he magnitude of [which] would depend on the specific timeframe of crossing the same waterbodies.”  Staff also concluded that concurrent construction “could have additive effects on surface water quality (e.g., turbidity, spills),” could “lead[] to alteration of water quality, depth, and flow rates” and could alter vegetation in ways that affect water quality” but concluded, overall, that “the [SSE] Project, when combined with other actions in geographic and temporal scope, would not have a significant cumulative effect on surface waters and wetlands.”  The Certificate Order, adopting this rationale, explained that the Commission agreed with the EA’s conclusion and affirmed the staff’s cumulative-effects analysis as sufficiently detailed.
Moreover, this finding is consistent with the Commission’s response to Petitioners’ similar claims in the Southgate Amendment Project proceeding, where the Commission recently explained that it evaluated cumulative effects of both projects, and found that “with appropriate BMPs in place, effects on waterbodies and wetlands would be minimized” and its conclusion that “the [Southgate] Amendment Project’s cumulative effects, including on wetlands and waterbodies, when considered with other projects would be less than significant.”
Petitioners attempt to find error in this analysis, contending that “the cumulative effect of a project would never be deemed significant unless that project and/or nearby construction projects violated their permit terms or applicable laws.”  We disagree.  The Commission’s evaluation of the cumulative effects on aquatic resources between the SSE Project and the Southgate Amendment Project was thorough and appropriately identified potential short- to long-term effects on aquatic resources in a specified geographic area where construction and operations may overlap.  “The NEPA process involves an almost endless series of judgment calls” that are vested in the agencies.  And “[w]hile additional data might enable a more detailed environmental analysis, NEPA does not require maximum detail” but instead, “requires agencies to make a series of  line-drawing decisions based on the significance and usefulness of additional information.”  Moreover, that the Commission approved project specific plans and mitigation measures in both proceedings is not an error.  Rather, the Commission appropriately identified quantifiable effects and measures that would reduce those effects to less than significant levels.  Accordingly, the Commission adequately considered cumulative effects on aquatic resources.
Greenhouse Gas Emissions
Petitioners take issue with both how the Commission considered GHG emissions under NEPA as well as under the NGA.  Petitioners claim that with regard to the project’s GHG emissions (including downstream emissions), “the Commission arbitrarily failed to consider harms from GHG emissions in its public interest balancing.”  Petitioners further claim that “the Commission concluded that the Project’s benefits outweighed its adverse impacts because it determined that the impacts were not significant, despite never making a determination as to whether the GHG impacts were significant.”  Accordingly, Petitioners argue that “the Commission cannot rationally conclude that the project’s benefits outweigh its harms on the basis that all of the harms are insignificant.”  Petitioners further contend that it was arbitrary to “consider end users’ downstream use of the gas as a benefit while assigning no weight to the tens of billions of dollars in damages that the resulting emissions could impose.”  We find these arguments unpersuasive and further find that these arguments have already been rejected by the courts.
The Commission considered the SSE Project’s GHG and climate impacts on a case-specific basis consistent with precedent.  As to Petitioners’ arguments regarding downstream GHG emissions, in the Certificate Order, the Commission pointed to the Supreme Court’s decision in Seven County, which explains that under NEPA, agencies “are not required to analyze the effects of projects over which they do not exercise regulatory authority,” which here would include downstream GHG emissions.  Petitioners, in their rehearing request, attempt to distinguish Seven County by claiming that the Commission should have considered the downstream emissions pursuant to its obligations under NGA section 7, separate from NEPA, but this reasoning has been expressly rejected by the D.C. Circuit, as discussed in detail below.
The D.C. Circuit has affirmed the Commission’s determination that it cannot make a significance finding as to GHGs where, as here, the Commission explained why it cannot make a GHG significance determination.  In any event, neither the Commission, nor any other federal agency, has identified criteria or a scientifically accepted tool or method that would enable the Commission to determine the significance of reasonably foreseeable GHG emissions.  Relevant here, the Certificate Order found, based on staff’s analysis in the EA, that “to date, the Commission has not identified a way to estimate discrete, quantifiable, physical impacts on the environment resulting from the project’s incremental contribution to GHGs... [and] [w]ithout the ability to determine discrete resource impacts, the Commission is unable to assess the project’s contribution to climate change through any objective analysis of physical impact attributable to the project.”  The Commission adopted staff’s position in the EA that it could not be determined “whether the effects from GHG emissions attributable to the project would be significant or insignificant.”  The Commission further “note[d] that NEPA does not require that the Commission formally label project-related GHG emissions as significant or insignificant.”  And Petitioners’ argument that the Commission erred by declining to make a significance finding as to GHGs “fare[s] no better” when framed as a challenge under the NGA.
As the D.C. Circuit recognized in Driftwood, “[j]ust because [the Commission] refused to resolve the significance of the emissions does not mean that [the Commission] refused to consider the emissions at all.”  As the Commission has explained, the NGA is the Commission’s “substantive statute.”  The purpose of NEPA is to integrate environmental review into the agency decision-making process to ensure that “environmental values and consequences have been considered during the planning stage of agency actions.”  In conducting its NGA balancing, the Commission balances the need for and benefits derived from the project against the potential adverse consequences, including environmental impacts identified in the NEPA document developed for the project within its purview.  As the D.C. Circuit affirmed, the Commission satisfies its NGA responsibilities and properly considered the effects of GHG emissions when balancing the project’s benefits against its costs by “discuss[ing] the project’s contributions to [GHG] emissions in its environmental impact statement, conclud[ing] that the project was ‘environmentally acceptable,’ and referenc[ing] that determination in its balancing.”
The Commission’s consideration of the SSE Project aligns with the analysis affirmed by the court in Driftwood.  Specifically, the Commission observed the SSE Project’s purpose to provide 1,596,900 Dth/d of incremental firm transportation service as well as improve the reliability of Transco’s system, and determined that the SSE Project would have no adverse impacts on existing shippers and other pipelines and their existing customers.  The Commission also considered comments in support of the SSE Project from the largest project shipper, Duke Energy, as well as comments from other stakeholders concerning the “need[] to bring more natural gas to the region, alleviate constraints, support economic development, and provide reliability.”  The Commission discussed the project’s contributions to GHG emissions, among other environmental impacts, in the EA, and referenced the discussions of the environmental impacts in its balancing in the Certificate Order.
Thus, although the SSE Project would have some environmental impacts, overall, the project fulfills the NGA’s core mandate of ensuring plentiful supplies of natural gas at reasonable prices, without resulting in identifiable significant environmental impacts.  Therefore, based on the record before us, we continue to find that on balance the SSE Project is required by the public convenience and necessity.
Next, Petitioners claim that the Commission “failed to meaningfully address issues ... regarding blowdown and fugitive greenhouse gas emissions estimates” and failed to “independently assess blowdown and fugitive emissions associated with the compressor stations and pipeline segments” and instead “uncritically adopted Transco’s estimates.”  We disagree.
In the EA, Commission staff analyzed blowdown emissions, noting that “[a]dditional sources of operational emissions for the [SSE] Project include fugitives and blowdowns associated with pigging operations along the pipelines” and that “[e]missions from pipeline blowdowns would also occur when natural gas is purged prior to pipeline maintenance or repair.”  The EA also disclosed these emissions in table B.7-3, titled “Summary of Annual Project Operational P[otential] T[o] E[mit] Emissions for Pipeline Fugitives and Venting.”
In the Certificate Order, the Commission directly responded to Petitioners’ claims, noting that “Commission staff performed a thorough review” of the expected air emissions including information provided by Transco in response to Commission staff’s requests for further data.  Moreover, the Commission confirmed that operational emissions would be in compliance with all applicable federal and state air regulations.
Petitioners further claim that the Commission may not use the methodology submitted by Transco, but fail to explain why that methodology is flawed, other than to generally allege that the methodology is not current when considering “recent studies showing that fugitive emissions occur along all steps of the gas supply chain and are often far greater than estimated.”  Petitioners’ assertions are not persuasive because Petitioners fail to explain how the referenced studies (which criticize use of existing EPA-based pipeline fugitive emissions factors generally) undermine the methodology and project-specific data analyzed by the Commission here, or how the measures that Transco will implement, discussed below, are insufficient.  
Moreover, the Commission’s choice among reasonable analytical methodologies is entitled to deference.  Regarding direct operational fugitive and blowdown emissions, the Commission appropriately requires that all projects be designed to meet the minimum standards that are set by the EPA, the agency that establishes air emission standards for stationary sources.  In addition, as described in the EA, Transco implements measures to reduce fugitive emissions from its natural gas operations, such as employing a leak detection and repair program and rerouting or capturing and recompressing natural gas during specific planned blowdowns.  Moreover, regarding upstream or downstream emissions, the Commission has explained, “there is no standard method for determining fugitive emissions for pipelines and the level of fugitive releases during the lifecycle of natural gas are highly debated, and, therefore, difficult to quantify.”  Regardless, in the wake of the Supreme Court’s decision in Seven County, upstream and downstream lifecycle analysis of indirect and cumulative impacts of fugitive emissions is no longer required.  Accordingly, we reaffirm that Commission’s consideration of fugitive and blowdown emissions in the EA and the Certificate Order was reasonable.
Finally, Petitioners contend that the Commission may not rely on state integrated resource plans “to validate ... underlying load-growth ... then treat[] state climate mandates ... as effectively irrelevant to its NGA Section 7 public interest balancing.”  Specifically, according to Petitioners, the Commission credited the state integrated resource planning process, while ignoring concerns expressed by a group of North Carolina legislators who “highlighted that SSE [Project] would enable combustion of downstream gas on the order of tens of millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO₂e) annually for decades, potentially imped[ing] the State’s decarbonization objectives and imposing long-lasting ratepayer burdens.”  We disagree.
The EA identified the comment letter received from North Carolina legislators and the Certificate Order discussed comments “argu[ing] that the project interferes with a North Carolina state law that requires Duke Energy to reduce carbon emissions.”  Although the Commission observed that “the project is not inconsistent with state utility goals,” this observation did not defer to state utility regulations on the one hand, without considering state carbon reduction laws on the other.  Rather, the Commission discussed GHG emissions in relation to state mandates in the EA while also explaining its limitations in both areas in the Certificate Order, “not[ing] that a state’s emission reductions goals or laws relate to the end-use of gas over which the Commission does not exercise regulatory authority” and that “[t]he Commission does not regulate states’ chosen mix of energy generation resources.”  Even with these statutory limitations, the Commission held, citing Transcon. Gas Pipe Line Co., that “natural gas transportation projects, such as this one, are not inherently incompatible with a state statute requiring a reduction in the average annual use of natural gas or in [GHG] emissions.”  Further, the Commission considered project GHG emissions while also observing “[w]ith respect to air quality impacts of burning natural gas for power generation,” that the Commission “[is] not required to consider in [a] NEPA analysis indirect, downstream emissions from the end use of transported gas as those are effects over which the Commission does not exercise regulatory authority.”  With these considerations in mind, the Commission “recognize[d] that the proposed project would impact the environment and individuals living in the vicinity of the project facilities” but ultimately held that “the project impacts, as mitigated, would not be significant” and “conclude[d] that, under section 7 of the NGA that, the public convenience and necessity requires approval of project.”
EA vs. EIS
Petitioners claim that the Commission ignored its comments on preparing an “EIS rather than a less comprehensive EA if a major federal action significantly affects the environment.”  Petitioners claim that the SSE Project warrants an EIS because the project “could cost the public approximately $87 billion from the societal costs of its greenhouse gas emissions ... [for] twenty operational years ...[and where] pipelines are ... designed to be used for fifty years ... the societal cost of SSEP [is] hundreds of billions of dollars.”  Issuance of an EA here, Petitioners claim, necessarily means that the Commission failed to take the required “hard look” at project impacts.  We disagree.
As explained in the Certificate Order, “NEPA requires that a federal agency prepare an EIS if the proposed agency action has a reasonably foreseeable significant impact on the quality of the human environment; [h]owever, an agency may prepare an EA if the proposed action does not have a reasonably foreseeable significant effect on the quality of the human environment or if the significance of such effect is unknown.”  An agency’s decision whether to prepare an EIS is left to its discretion.
Contrary to Petitioners’ claims, Commission staff considered Petitioners’ comments and whether the project required an EIS, as is required by Commission regulations.  Specifically, as discussed in the EA:
The Commission’s regulations at 18 CFR 306(b) state that “If the Commission believes that a proposed action…may not be a major federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment, an EA, rather than an EIS, will be prepared first.  Depending on the outcome of the EA, an EIS may or may not be prepared.”  In preparing this EA, we are fulfilling our obligation under NEPA to consider and disclose the environmental effects of the [SSE] Project.  Based on our analysis and considering that the [SSE] Project would primarily involve pipeline looping and modifications to existing facilities, we conclude ... that the [SSE] Project effects would not be significant, and thus, an EA is warranted. 
Further, as the Commission explained in the Certificate Order, after assessing information obtained during the scoping period, staff prepared an EA “because neither the application nor comments during the scoping process identified the potential for significant effects, which was confirmed by the environmental review process.”  Accordingly, the Commission appropriately found that no EIS was required given that “project construction, abandonment, and operation would not constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.”
Next, Petitioners contend that the Commission is required to prepare an EIS because the Commission “has routinely prepared [an EIS] for smaller pipeline projects” in relation to the SSE Project and because an EIS “would have enabled the Commission to adequately analyze, disclose, and mitigate the [SSE] Project’s adverse consequences, and to better weigh them against ... purported public benefits” and a “more thorough analysis” of the environmental impacts of the SSE Project.  We disagree.
As noted in the Supreme Court’s decision in Seven County, “agencies determine whether and to what extent to prepare an EIS based on the usefulness of any new potential information to the decisionmaking process.”  Moreover, “NEPA is a procedural cross-check, not a substantive roadblock … [and] [t]he goal of the law is to inform agency decisionmaking, not to paralyze it.”  Commission staff prepared a comprehensive and detailed assessment of environmental effects in the EA, considering at length – in more than 750 pages of analysis including exhibits and tables – the environmental effects of the project in all resource areas, project alternatives, including the no-action alternative, and cumulative effects, including GHG and climate change effects.  Staff also recommended sixteen mandatory environmental conditions to mitigate potential environmental impacts, which the Commission considered and adopted along with the EA’s finding of no significant impact.  This approach is consistent with NEPA.
Moreover, Petitioners’ claim that the Commission arbitrarily prepared an EA, when it has prepared an EIS for “smaller” projects in the past, relies on selectively extrapolated geographic footprint and physical attribute data that Petitioners then compare to the physical attribute data of other projects.  However, that method for determining whether an EIS is required is not grounded in NEPA.
Specifically, Petitioners’ failure to reference any effects that flow from these attributes renders its analysis flawed.  For example, Petitioners compare pipeline length, compression horsepower and “dekatherms per day for which [the Commission] has previously prepared an EIS,” and suggest that an EIS is required because the project “has the third-highest capacity, sixth most miles of pipeline constructed, ... [and] greatest increase in horsepower at its various compressor stations.”  However, Petitioners fail to explain how these attributes correlate to the statutory standard for preparing an EIS, namely whether the project has a “reasonably foreseeable significant impact on the quality of the human environment.”  Nor do they address the numerous mitigation measures discussed in the EA, or the environmental advantages of co-locating with existing pipelines, or explain what specifically about the acreage impacted renders the impacts “significant.”  Accordingly, recognizing that the decision whether to prepare an EA or an EIS is left to agency discretion, is highly project-specific, and necessarily focuses on the potential impacts of the project not the project’s physical attributes or size, we continue to find that the Commission appropriately prepared an EA for the SSE Project.
The Commission orders:

In response to Petitioners’ request for rehearing, the Certificate Order is hereby modified and set aside, in part, as discussed in the body of this order.
By the Commission.
